text: Add a compatibility-corpus register (C-IDs) defining L0–L5 and W1–W3 with sizes, scenario scripts, rating scales and per-milestone thresholds.
Add an invariants register (I-IDs) for standing rules, each with the lint or test task that enforces it.
Define a written license firewall that maps each stability layer to a license class: Layer 1 kernel GPLv2, Layers 2-4 permissive.
rationale: It mirrors the architectural firewall and prevents copyleft from leaking upward into platform interfaces and the SDK.

text: Decide the license for native userspace platform services (compositor, package manager, personality glue, system services) among MIT, Apache-2.0, MPL-2.0 and dual MIT/Apache-2.0, including whether an explicit patent grant is required.
rationale: Every service written from V0.5 onward needs a header on day one and retroactive relicensing needs every contributor's consent.

text: Produce a machine-readable SBOM (SPDX or CycloneDX) for the kernel, every package and every system generation, keyed by content hash.
rationale: GPL corresponding-source obligations and the EU Cyber Resilience Act both require knowing exactly what shipped.

text: Build a license-scanning pipeline over all vendored and dependency sources with a zero-unknown-license CI gate.
rationale: Manual review does not scale to a kernel fork plus a package ecosystem.

text: Publish a userspace dependency license allowlist that excludes AGPL, SSPL, BUSL and similar source-available licenses from the default image and SDK dependency tree.
rationale: Network-copyleft and non-open licenses would impose obligations on users and application developers that the platform cannot honor.

text: Establish a patent-encumbered codec policy (H.264, HEVC, AAC, Dolby) covering software decoders, hardware passthrough and jurisdiction-dependent packaging.
rationale: A desktop that cannot play common media is unusable, but shipping encumbered decoders without a policy creates royalty exposure.

text: Run a trademark clearance search for the project name across major jurisdictions and register word and logo marks before any public release.
rationale: Renaming after a public alpha destroys recognition and invites squatting.

text: Publish a trademark usage policy for derivatives, spins, merchandise and compatible-with claims modeled on Debian, Fedora and Rust policies.
rationale: Without a policy the mark either cannot be enforced or blocks legitimate community use.

text: Decide whether Linux appears in any product naming and, if so, obtain the Linux Mark Institute sublicense.
rationale: Linux is a registered trademark and Linux-derived is a claim that must be worded carefully.

text: Define rules for referring to Windows, Steam, Proton and other third-party marks in compatibility documentation and marketing.
rationale: Compatibility claims are the most trademark-sensitive statements the project will make.

text: Register the project's domains, package repository namespace, code-hosting organisation and social handles under the legal entity rather than an individual.
rationale: Infrastructure owned by one person is a single point of failure for a multi-year project.

text: Adopt DCO Signed-off-by for kernel contributions and decide between DCO and a non-assignment CLA for userspace, recorded as an ADR.
rationale: Contribution provenance must be captured from the first commit because it cannot be reconstructed later.

text: Define an AI-assisted contribution policy covering disclosure, provenance, license compatibility of generated code and reviewer responsibility.
rationale: The project is tracked and partly implemented by AI agents, and upstream Linux and others are adopting such rules that the fork must interoperate with.

text: Decide the copyright holder model (contributors retain copyright versus assignment to an entity) and whether any relicensing clause exists.
rationale: This determines whether license corrections are ever possible and whether external contributors will participate.

text: Decide whether and when to form a legal entity (foundation, fiscal sponsor or company) able to hold trademarks and signing keys and to sign vendor agreements.
rationale: Shim signing, anti-cheat agreements, OIN membership and donations all require a counterparty.

text: Which jurisdiction should the legal entity be in, considering export controls, GDPR, trademark cost and tax treatment of donations?
rationale: Jurisdiction shapes every later compliance obligation and is expensive to change.

text: File the publicly-available encryption source notification under EAR 742.15(b) and document export-control classification for releases containing disk encryption and TLS.
rationale: Public binary distribution of cryptography from or through the US requires the notice to use the open-source exception.

text: Define the RFC process: stages, templates, discussion venues, final-comment period, decision authority and timeboxes.
rationale: Architecture decisions spanning decades need a repeatable, recorded process from V0.

text: Define the ADR template and lifecycle (proposed, accepted, superseded, deprecated) with a mandatory options-considered section and linkage to task IDs.
rationale: ADR tasks are a planning assumption but their format and lifecycle are undefined.

text: Publish a 1.0 stability contract stating which ABIs and interfaces are frozen, the support lifecycle, and what constitutes a breaking change.
rationale: A stable release is a promise and the promise must be written down.

text: Adopt a governance charter: decision model (BDFL, council or foundation TSC), maintainer appointment and removal, voting and conflict resolution.
rationale: External contributors will not invest without knowing how decisions are made.

text: Maintain a MAINTAINERS/CODEOWNERS mapping per workstream with review requirements enforced by the forge.
rationale: Thirty workstreams need explicit ownership for reviews and gate sign-off.

text: Adopt a Code of Conduct with a named enforcement body and escalation path before the repository opens to external contributors.
rationale: Public projects without one lose contributors at the first incident.

text: Publish CONTRIBUTING guidance covering commit conventions, review expectations, response-time targets and how to propose or modify tasks in the tracking repository.
rationale: The Markdown task repository is the coordination surface and needs rules for humans and agents alike.

text: Define a vendor influence and conflict-of-interest policy for hardware vendors, game platforms and sponsors.
rationale: Target-hardware selection and gaming partnerships create obvious capture risks.

text: Decide the funding model (donations, sponsorship tiers, fiscal sponsor) and publish transparent finances.
rationale: Hardware, CI capacity and signing infrastructure cost money before V2.

text: Define milestone gate governance: who approves gate exit, evidence required, and how milestones are re-scoped or tasks dropped.
rationale: Gates and exit criteria exist as files but need an owner and a process to be meaningful.

text: Define the research program process: timeboxed spikes, evaluation against the litmus test, graduation to ADR, and kill criteria.
rationale: The inspiration list becomes wasted effort without a way to convert research into decisions.

text: Stand up community infrastructure (issue tracker, forum, chat, mailing lists) with a moderation policy and archive guarantees.
rationale: Public alpha users need somewhere to report and discuss.

text: Publish an issue triage policy with labels, severity definitions, response targets and stale handling.
rationale: A public tracker without triage rules becomes noise within weeks.

text: Decide the documentation license (CC-BY-SA, CC-BY or CC0) and the terms for translation contributions.
rationale: Documentation is a V3 requirement and translations are contributions with their own licensing.

text: License the task-tracking and decisions repository itself and state the license of ADR content.
rationale: The planning corpus will be read and forked by others and needs clear terms from the start.

text: Publish a downstream and derivative-distribution policy covering rebranding requirements, unofficial builds and use of the official package repository.
rationale: Beta-stage spins will appear and need rules that protect users and the mark.

text: Decide on Open Invention Network membership and a defensive patent pledge for the project entity.
rationale: Patent exposure grows with public distribution and OIN membership is the standard mitigation for Linux-derived systems.

text: Adopt a maintainer succession and continuity plan covering key escrow, admin access and bus factor for critical workstreams.
rationale: A multi-year project must survive the loss of any single maintainer.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Run licence compliance scanning in CI covering GPLv2 obligations for kernel code, crate licences, firmware redistribution terms and the Windows/Linux test corpus, with an ADR fixing the userspace licence choice.
rationale: Licence violations discovered at public alpha would block distribution of every artifact.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Assemble a legally reviewed test corpus of Linux applications, Windows applications and games, fonts, images and documents that CI is permitted to redistribute to runners.
rationale: Compatibility and parser testing need real inputs and most real inputs carry licences that forbid casual redistribution.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Build documentation and ADR CI: generate interface reference docs from IDL, check ADR cross-links and task ID references, and fail on broken links or unparseable task templates.
rationale: The Markdown repository is the source of truth for years of progress and its parseability must be enforced like code.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Commission an independent external security audit of the capability kernel, bootloader chain, disk encryption and identity/secrets services before 1.0, with findings tracked as tasks.
rationale: A new security model shipped as stable without outside review is asking users to trust unproven claims.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Publish a user-facing platform security guide stating exactly what the OS protects against (and does not) in each state: powered off, suspended, locked, unlocked, developer mode.
rationale: Users and reviewers will otherwise assume protections the design does not deliver, particularly around suspend and developer mode.

text: Codec shipping and patent policy: which codecs are in the default image (AV1, VP9, Opus, FLAC, Vorbis), which arrive via hardware decoders only (H.264, HEVC), and which are optional user-installed packages.
rationale: Patent exposure decides what a distributed 1.0 image may legally contain and users judge an OS by whether video plays.

text: Opt-in usage telemetry policy and implementation (what is collected, anonymisation, retention, user-visible toggle) separate from crash reporting.
rationale: A 1.0 project needs adoption and hardware data but any undisclosed collection would destroy the trust a capability-security OS depends on.

text: Decide whether to run a vulnerability reward program at 1.0 and how it is funded.
rationale: Reward programs materially change report volume and the triage capacity that must be staffed.

text: Resolve redistribution licensing for firmware blobs, microcode and proprietary drivers, deciding what ships in official images versus a separate non-free repository.
rationale: Shipping Wi-Fi and GPU firmware without redistribution rights blocks any public image.

text: Publish corresponding source for every GPL component of every released generation and automate the source offer from the content-addressed store.
rationale: A Linux kernel fork distributed publicly carries GPL obligations from the first download.

text: Decide code hosting (self-hosted forge versus GitHub) and repository layout (monorepo versus per-workstream repositories) including where the Markdown task repository lives.
rationale: Every CI, review and contribution process from V0 onward depends on this choice.

text: Decide contributor licensing terms (DCO versus CLA) and the outbound license for native kernel code alongside inherited GPLv2 code.
rationale: Mixing Rust native code with GPL Linux code has licensing consequences that must be settled before external contributions arrive.

text: Define issue triage: severity and priority labels, hardware and personality tags, templates that capture generation ID and diagnostics, response-time targets and a stale policy.
rationale: Public alpha issue volume will bury the team without a triage process defined earlier.

text: Stand up community channels (forum, chat, announcement feed, mailing list), a code of conduct and moderation roles before public alpha.
rationale: Public users need somewhere to ask questions that is not the issue tracker.

text: Publish a trademark and branding policy for derivatives, remixes and unofficial builds.
rationale: Immutable generations make remixing easy and users must be able to tell official builds from forks.

text: Assess export control and cryptography distribution obligations for the download site and mirrors.
rationale: An OS with disk encryption distributed worldwide has legal obligations that cannot be ignored at public alpha.

text: Estimate and plan funding for ongoing infrastructure cost (CDN bandwidth, build farm, hardware lab, signing hardware) through 1.0 and beyond.
rationale: Release infrastructure has recurring cost and a stable release implies it stays online.

text: Decide whether to pursue OEM partnerships or a hardware certification programme before 1.0 or leave it to post-1.0.
rationale: A certified machine is the strongest adoption vector but commits scarce engineering to vendor relations.

text: Decide the policy for shipping patent-encumbered codecs (H.264, HEVC, AAC) and proprietary fonts or font metric substitutes needed for migrated media and documents.
rationale: Migrated photo, video and document libraries are useless if the OS cannot decode or render them, and the legal answer differs by jurisdiction.

text: Publish a user-facing support matrix and decision tree describing where a given application runs (native, Linux personality, Windows personality, fallback VM, not at all) and the expected experience in each.
rationale: Users decide to switch based on whether their specific software works, and a single honest page answers that.

text: Do not build another Linux distribution; the project identity and gating must reject distribution-style deliverables.
Do not build another desktop environment on top of an existing Linux userspace.
Publish a vision document stating what the project is and is not building, as the top-level entry point of the repository.
Preserve mature Linux mechanisms and replace only inherited semantics; every subsystem task must classify its target as mechanism (keep) or semantics (replace).
Compatibility personalities inherit history; native software does not. This firewall must be documented and enforced in ABI review.
Publish the high-level architecture diagram and layer definitions as a maintained document with each layer's owning workstream.
Resolve which kernel evolution phase (C, D or E) is a hard requirement for the 1.0 release gate.
The 20 ms startup figure must be documented as a measurement target, not an architectural guarantee, in all public material.
Establish a 'fossilization review' checklist applied to every native ABI change, checking each §38 assumption explicitly.
Decide the 1.0 portability commitment: x86-64 only as a shipping target while the ABI remains architecture-neutral (ADR).
Decide governance of a standard semantic interface catalogue (Document, Mail, Calendar, Project) and who may extend it (ADR, RFC process).
Complete a licence review for Wine (LGPL), DXVK, VKD3D-Proton and related components used by the Windows personality.
Write SDK documentation, API reference and tutorials for the reference example (window, choose image, decode, render).
Do not set or communicate a goal of 'everything is 2x faster than Linux'; Linux is already extremely fast and the goal is semantic elimination of cost, not uniform speedup.
Design reviews must apply the rule 'don't merely optimise expensive abstractions; remove the need for them' and record which abstraction a proposal eliminates.
No documentation, release note or announcement may claim performance superiority without linking to the measurement and its methodology.
Kernel fork maintenance is a permanent engineering cost; the project must document staffing and process for it before Phase D divergence.
No OS wins solely because its kernel is beautiful; every milestone gate from V1 onward must include ecosystem criteria, not only kernel criteria.
Documentation for users, developers and contributors.
Compatibility is existential: ecosystem gaps must be filled through personalities before native alternatives exist; no ecosystem gap may be left open pending a native rewrite.
Do not promise impossible speedups in any public communication.
Encode the §57 list as a mandatory design-review checklist attached to the ADR template.
Research program: one comparative-study document per inspiration in a research/ directory; every ADR must cite the relevant prior art studied.
The acceptance test for borrowing an idea is 'does it produce the strongest coherent system', never pedigree, novelty or ecosystem fashion.
V0 exit criteria must explicitly state that V0 is not a usable desktop and must not include any UI or desktop deliverable.
V0 milestone file with gate and exit criteria mapping every §59 required item and measurement.
V0.5 exit criterion: the application model is proven by four demo native applications running on the native compositor from immutable packages.
V0.5 milestone file with gate and exit criteria mapping every §60 item.
V1 exit criterion: the OS is useful enough that its developers build the OS while running the OS (self-hosting).
Daily-driving internally is mandatory from V1; track dogfooding adoption and blockers as milestone metrics.
V1 milestone file with gate and exit criteria mapping every §61 item.
V2 milestone file with gate and exit criteria mapping every §62 item.
V3 targets enthusiasts, developers, OS researchers and experimenting gamers; documentation, onboarding and messaging must be written for that audience.
Documentation: installation, user guide, developer guide, compatibility guide, contributor guide.
V3 milestone file with gate and exit criteria mapping every §63 item.
The baseline defines no criteria for V4 beta or 1.0 stable; define them (stability SLOs, security audit, ABI freeze, LTS/support commitment, hardware list, compatibility pass rates).
ABI review process with a higher approval bar than SDK changes, recorded in governance.
Documented stability policy per layer: allowed change types, deprecation windows, support duration.
High-level ideas must live in Layer 3/4 so they are not frozen forever; a concept may only move down a layer via ADR.
Principle 1: compatibility is a subsystem, not the architecture; personalities may not add native ABI surface.
Principle 2: preserve mature mechanisms, replace inherited semantics.
Principle 15: never replace something mature unless the new model provides meaningful, measured benefit.
Principle 16: do not chase novelty for its own sake.
Principle 17: do not optimise expensive abstractions when they can be eliminated.
Publish PRINCIPLES.md; the ADR template must require citing which principles a decision upholds and which it trades off.
ADR template must include the two litmus-test questions: 'best model we know today or because Unix/Windows/Linux did it?' and 'replacing something mature merely because ours feels newer?'.
Any subsystem design whose litmus answer is 'history' must be reconsidered and the reconsideration recorded in the ADR.
Any subsystem design that replaces a mature component must justify the replacement with measurable benefit in the ADR.
'Compatibility software gets the past, native software gets the future': personalities consume the native ABI but never extend it with legacy semantics.
Living architecture document reproducing the §69 diagram, with every box linked to its owning workstream and current status.
Write the project charter (MISSION.md) adopting the §70 mission statement.

Each mission pillar — capabilities, cheap isolated components, structured asynchronous execution, typed interfaces, transferable memory ownership, immutable system state, heterogeneous compute, semantic automation, hardware-independent abstractions — must map to a workstream with explicit 1.0 exit criteria.
1.0 exit criteria must include compatibility UX criteria proving Linux and Windows software feel like native citizens (cross-ref §49).
